extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the MPEP/Alice two-step framework (MPEP 2106) to determine whether patent claims recite judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature) and whether the claims integrate those exceptions into a practical application. Includes claim interpretation and evaluation of additional elements (e.g., DNNs, data gathering, synthesis steps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation — broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification as interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art (MPEP 2111). The broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the disclosure is used to construe claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation examples: preamble reciting a non-transitory computer-readable storage medium is construed to cover statutory embodiments (random-access memory, flash, magnetic/optical storage) but not transitory signals. If a claim does not specify how a step is performed, that sub-step may be performed "as indicated in the specification or by any other method known to a person having ordinary skill in the art." Use the specification's definitions when present (e.g., "informative SNPs").

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category determination (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: First determine whether the claim falls within any statutory category of invention (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) per MPEP 2106.03.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a series of steps/acts is a "process" (Step 1: YES). A non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions is a "manufacture." Document the statutory category before proceeding to judicial-exception analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim 'recites' a judicial exception (Step 2A, Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim "recites" (i.e., sets forth or describes) a judicial exception such as a mathematical concept, mental process, or law of nature (MPEP 2106.04).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific limitations that align with at least one judicial exception. Examples from text: (b)-(e) recite mathematical concepts; partitioning embeddings may be a mental process. Use the claim language itself to determine whether the exception is set forth in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping of judicial exceptions and mapping claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Map claim limitations to the judicial-exception groupings: mathematical concepts, mental processes, laws of nature, and certain types of organizing human activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: k-means clustering, binary masking, arithmetic weighting and summing -> mathematical concepts; comparing a PRS to a top-quartile threshold -> mental process; the relationship between genotype and phenotype -> law of nature. Note that items may fall under multiple groupings; pick at least one for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider limitations together where possible (avoid over-parsing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, consider claim limitations together as a single abstract idea rather than parsing the claim into multiple separate exceptions (MPEP 2106.04 II.B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If steps (b)-(e) all fall within the mathematical-concepts grouping, analyze them together as a single abstract idea for Step 2A, Prong One. Do not artificially split limitations into multiple exceptions unless clearly distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A, Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application by (1) identifying any additional elements beyond the exception, and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination (MPEP 2106.04(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for elements that meaningfully limit the claim or reflect a technical improvement. Compare additional elements (e.g., synthesis into time-domain waveforms, specific conversions, use of ASR to obtain transcripts) against the abstract idea to determine whether the claim as a whole is directed to a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity / post-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-solution activities or nominal steps that merely transmit or store data, or otherwise occur after the solution, are insignificant additions that do not integrate the judicial exception (MPEP 2106.05(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "transmitting the mixed speech signal x' for storage to a remote location" is a post-solution step that "does not meaningfully limit the claim." Label such elements as insignificant extra-solution activity and do not treat them as integrating the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data gathering is an insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting samples or obtaining data (e.g., collecting and genotyping a sample to provide a genotype dataset) generally amounts to mere data gathering and is an insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP 2106.05(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat data-collection/genotyping steps as necessary preambles for using the judicial exception but not as meaningful limitations that integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to 'apply it' / use of a computer as a tool (MPEP 2106.05(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recited computer or ML model that only amounts to instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (i.e., "apply it") does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing generic recitations (e.g., "a DNN trained for source separation" with no structural detail), consider: (1) whether the claim recites only the idea/solution or outcome; (2) whether it invokes computers/machinery merely as a tool; and (3) the particularity or generality of the application. Generic ML recitations without specifics are likely mere implementation instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic field-of-use or technological-environment linking is insufficient (MPEP 2106.05(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Confining the use of an abstract idea to a particular technological environment by general linking (e.g., "use a DNN") does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad recital that ties the abstract idea to a field of use or technology without specifying how the technology is specifically used to solve a technical problem should be treated as an attempt to claim an abstract idea in a technological field rather than a meaningful integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical improvement to computer or other technology integrates the exception (MPEP 2106.05(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim reflects a concrete technical improvement to computer technology or another technology, or otherwise solves a technical problem using specific features described in the disclosure, the claim integrates the abstract idea into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: converting masked clusters into separate speech waveforms and generating a mixed speech signal that excludes an undesired source was treated as reflecting an improvement in speech-separation technology and thus integrates the abstract idea. Look for claim features that mirror the improvements described in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-mental, non-abstract physical/technical transformations are not judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim steps that require physical or technical transformations beyond what can be practically performed in the human mind are not mental-process abstract ideas (e.g., synthesizing waveforms, converting clusters to time-domain signals, ASR-generated transcripts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an element cannot be practically performed mentally and is not merely a mathematical concept described in text (e.g., no formula), treat it as a non-judicial-exception element that can help integrate the abstract idea into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts require specific formulae/relationships; mere variables may not suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim recites a mathematical concept when it sets forth mathematical operations/formulae/relationships (e.g., k-means clustering, arithmetic weighting). Merely reciting variables or naming an operation without mathematical detail may not itself be a mathematical concept recitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "stitching" could involve a mathematical overlap-add method, but if the claim recites no details (no formulae, no calculations), the combining step may be considered merely based on a mathematical concept rather than reciting a mathematical concept. Examine whether explicit formulae or calculational steps are claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of recitations that fall under multiple exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a limitation can be characterized under multiple judicial-exception categories, the examiner may identify it under at least one exception and proceed (MPEP 2106.04 I & II.B), but should be careful not to artificially fragment the claim into multiple separate exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a weighted PRS limitation may be a mathematical calculation, a mental process, and involve a law of nature; it suffices to peg it to at least one grouping for further analysis, while considering the limitations together where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-ability standard for mental-process classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify a limitation as a mental process if it can be practically performed in the human mind. The use of simple physical aids (pen and paper, calculator) does not negate the mental nature (MPEP 2106.04(a)(2) III.B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: evaluating whether a patient's PRS is in the top quartile or tallying and weighting alleles is treatable as a mental process because a human could in principle perform the calculations/assessments (even if aided by a calculator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility decision-flow labeling and outcomes (Step 2A results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Record and report the Step 2A determinations (Prong One: does the claim recite an exception? Prong Two: does the claim integrate the exception into a practical application?). The combination of prong outcomes determines whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Prong One identifies an abstract idea (YES) but Prong Two finds the claim integrates that idea into a practical application (YES), then the claim is not "directed to" the judicial exception and is eligible. If Prong Two is NO, the claim is directed to an abstract idea and further analysis under the inventive-concept framework may be required.
